q: 1. The structural analysis used in the ultimate strength design of R.C.C. structure is
explain: Even though we design for ultimate strength, the distribution of forces is still usually based on linear elastic analysis.

q: 2. The ultimate load used in the ultimate strength design of R.C.C. structures refers to
options: working loads multiplied by load factors
explain: Ultimate load = Characteristic Load × Load Factor.

q: 3. The ultimate strength of a balanced reinforced concrete beam is proportional to
options: crushing strength of an and/or tensile strength of the steel
explain: In a balanced section, both concrete and steel reach their limits simultaneously.

q: 4. The ultimate strength of an under reinforced R.C.C. beam is proportional to
options: crushing strength of the concrete and/or tensile strength of the steel
explain: The strength of an under-reinforced beam is limited by the amount of steel provided.

q: 5. The ultimate strength of an over reinforced R.C.C. beam is proportional to
options: crushing strength of the concrete and/or tensile strength of the steel
explain: In over-reinforced beams, concrete fails before the steel reaches its yield strength.

q: 6. The ultimate bending compressive strain allowed in R.C.C. beam is
explain: IS 456 assumes the maximum strain in concrete at the outermost compression fiber is 0.0035 in bending.

q: 7. The primary compression failure in R.C.C. beam is caused in
explain: Over-reinforced beams fail suddenly due to concrete crushing (primary compression failure).

q: 8. The secondary compression failure in R.C.C. beam is caused in
explain: In under-reinforced beams, steel yields first, causing the neutral axis to rise until concrete crushes (secondary compression failure).

q: 9. The ratio of the allowable ultimate crushing stress of beam in bending to that of 150 mm cube strength is
explain: Due to size effect and difference between lab and site, strength in the structure is taken as 0.67fck.

q: 10. For a balanced design, according to I.S. : 456, the maximum depth of concrete stress block in R.C.C. beams should be
explain: For Fe250 steel, the limiting neutral axis depth (Xu,max) is 0.53d.

q: 11. The combined load factor applied in the ultimate strength design of R.C.C. structures is
explain: The most common partial safety factor for loads (Dead Load + Live Load) is 1.5.

q: 12. A pre-stressed concrete member
explain: Pre-stressed concrete is defined by the intentional introduction of internal stresses (usually compressive) to counteract the tensile stresses caused by external loads.

q: 13. In a prestressed member it is advisable to use
options: low strength concrete but high tensile steel
high strength concrete and high tensile steel
explain: High strength concrete is needed to resist high bearing stresses at anchorages and minimize creep/shrinkage losses, while high tensile steel is required to maintain effective prestress after accounting for various losses.

q: 14. Post tensioning system
options: was widely used in earlier days
is not economical and hence not generally used
is economical for large spans and is adopted now a days
explain: Post-tensioning allows for thinner slabs and longer spans without intermediate columns, making it highly economical for bridges and large commercial buildings today.

q: 15. In prestressed concrete structures the prestressing of the concrete is done to compensate the stresses caused by
explain: Prestressing is designed to counteract the tensile stresses produced by the total working loads (the combination of dead and live loads) during the service life of the structure.

q: 16. The net effect due to prestressing in prestressed concrete beams is usually
explain: Prestressing introduces a longitudinal compressive force and a bending moment (due to eccentricity) which counteracts the downward bending from external loads.

q: 17. Prestressing in concrete beams is usually obtained by
explain: Most prestressed concrete involves internal prestressing, where tendons are placed within the concrete section (either pre-tensioned or post-tensioned in ducts).

q: 18. When the pile is suspended from two points, the minimum B.M. will occur if the overhang from each support is
explain: For a beam or pile suspended at two points, the maximum positive and negative bending moments are minimized when the overhang is approximately 0.207L (often rounded to 0.206L).

q: 19. The length of a reinforced concrete pile is taken as ............ the length embedded in firm stratum.
explain: In certain design simplified assumptions, the effective length of the pile is taken as half of the total length if the soil provides significant lateral restraint.

q: 20. The ultimate moment resisting capacity of a simple supported pre-stressed concreted beam is obtained by using
options: stress-strain relationship of concrete and steel
explain: The analysis of prestressed sections at the ultimate limit state requires satisfying both equilibrium of forces and the compatibility of strains between steel and concrete.

q: 21. The major loss of pre-stress is caused due to
explain: Loss of prestress occurs due to immediate factors (elastic shortening) and time-dependent factors (creep, shrinkage, and steel relaxation).

q: 22. Columns may be made of plain concrete of their unsupported length do not exceed their least lateral dimension
explain: According to IS 456, a compression member is called a 'pedestal' if its unsupported length is less than 3 times its least lateral dimension; these can be plain concrete.

q: 23. The modular ratio m of a concrete whose permissible compressive stress is C, may be obtained from the equation
explain: The standard IS 456 formula for the modular ratio in Working Stress Method is m = 280 / (3 * sigma_cbc), where C is the permissible stress.

q: 24. For M 150 grade concrete (1 : 2 : 4) the moment of resistance factor is
explain: The Q factor (Moment of Resistance factor) for M15 grade concrete in WSM (balanced section) is approximately 8.5.

q: 25. The percentage minimum reinforcement of the gross sectional area in slabs, is
explain: IS 456 specifies 0.15% for mild steel bars and 0.12% for HYSD bars. 0.15% is the standard general minimum.

q: 26. The weight of reinforced concrete, is generally taken as
explain: Plain concrete is 2400 kg/m³, while reinforced concrete (RCC) is taken as 2500 kg/m³ to account for the higher density of steel.

q: 27. If the ratio of the span to the overall depth does not exceed 10, the stiffness of the beam will ordinarily be satisfactory in case of a
explain: Cantilever beams are most critical for deflection; keeping L/D ≤ 10 (or specifically 7 for basic limits) usually ensures adequate stiffness.

q: 28. The ratio of the breadth to effective depth of a beam is kept
explain: For economical and structural efficiency, the breadth of a beam is typically half (0.50) of its effective depth.

q: 29. An under-reinforced section means
options: steel is provided at the underside only
steel provided on one face only
explain: In an under-reinforced section, the steel reaches its yield stress before the concrete reaches its maximum compressive strain, providing ductile failure.

q: 30. Design of R.C.C. simply supported beams carrying U.D.L. is based on the resultant B.M. at
explain: For a simply supported beam with UDL, the maximum bending moment (wl²/8) occurs at the mid-span, which governs the flexural design.

q: 31. Steel beam theory is used for
options: doubly reinforced beams ignoring compressive stress in concrete
beams if shear exceeds 4 times allowable shear stress
explain: Steel beam theory assumes that all compressive and tensile forces are carried by the steel reinforcement, ignoring the contribution of concrete in the compression zone.
